amendments.rule: The conjunction `וְ` is normally English *and*, including the waw of a consecutive verb form: the conjunction takes *And* and the verb takes the verb. Where the ASV renders it by some other connective, align it to that word instead. **The list is open and is read off the ASV rather than checked against a set**: the corpus already aligns a waw to *but*, *then*, *so*, *or*, *now*, *also*, *for*, *therefore*, *neither*, *nor*, *yea*, *yet*, *even*, *with*, *moreover* and *howbeit*, among others. A connective the ASV has written for a waw is never `added`, and it is never folded into a neighbouring word to avoid one: a town list writes *with* for the waw of `וְחַצְרֵיהֶן` → *with their villages* and *even* for the waw of `וָיָמָּה` → *even unto the sea*, and each waw takes the word written for it. **Where the ASV renders one connective morpheme by a correlative pair such as *both … and*, *either … or* or *whether … or*, both English words belong to that morpheme's one discontinuous unit, headed on the closing connective (*and* or *or*); the opening correlative is not `added`.** **This governs the disjunctive `אוֹ` exactly as it governs a waw**, since what licenses the pair is the one connective the ASV has rendered by it and not the lemma: `לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה` → ***whether*** *a male* ***or*** *a female* gives *whether … or* to the single `אוֹ`, headed on *or*. Where the Hebrew instead writes a connective of its own for each member — `אוֹ … אוֹ` → *either … or* — each takes only the English word written for it and there is no pair to place. **But that governs only a pair no other morpheme has a claim on.** Where another morpheme standing in the clause is itself what the opening correlative says — a present negative for the *neither* of *neither … nor*, the `מִן` of a `מִן … עַד` range for the *both* of *both … and* — that morpheme takes the opening word and the waw takes only the closing connective, exactly as rule 47 gives a written *the* to a present article before a supplied one and rule 46 gives a *that* to a present relative before a bare participle. `אֲשֶׁר לֹא־יָדְעוּ הֵמָּה וַאֲבוֹתָם` → *whom* ***neither*** *they* ***nor*** *their fathers have known* gives *neither* to `לֹא` and *nor* to the waw, and `מֵעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה` → ***both*** *the birds of the heavens* ***and*** *the beasts* gives *both* to `מִן` and *and* to the waw, leaving the `עַד` `unrepresented` under rule 40. **A morpheme that merely stands where the opening correlative stands has no claim on it.** What gives another morpheme that word is that the morpheme is itself what the correlative says, so read sense and not position: the two `לְ`s of `לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה` stand exactly where an English *whether* and a second *for* would stand, and a benefactive preposition is not what *whether* says, so both are `unrepresented` under rule 40 and neither takes the word. Count the correlative's members against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. This does not touch rule 35's fusion, which is a single English word carrying every morpheme's sense: a lone *Nor* or *neither* with no answering *nor* written is that rule's, and only a written pair is this one's. **And a pair is written only where the opening correlative stands before the first member.** Where the ASV instead postposes a floating *both* after the coordinated members, no correlative pair is written and the word is not the waw's: the waw takes the *and* written for it, and the *both* is its own `added` unit under rule 30, for the reason rule 51 gives about a second English word offered to a waw that already holds one. `אֹתוֹ וְאֶת־בְּנוֹ לֹא תִשְׁחֲטוּ בְּיוֹם אֶחָד` → *ye shall not kill it and its young* ***both*** *in one day* leaves its *both* `added`, while the *both* of `מֵעוֹף הַשָּׁמַיִם וְעַד־בְּהֵמָה` above is written where the pair opens and is placed as that sentence directs. Read the English word order, since what tells the two apart is where the ASV has put the opening word and not that it has written one. Read what stands in the clause for that waw in particular, as rule 51 requires for *also*, and where the ASV leaves it unrendered, mark it `unrepresented`. **But read whether a waw is present at all before placing the connective.** Where the ASV writes a coordinating *and*, *or* or *but*, or a resumptive apodosis connective such as *then*, *so* or *therefore*, for a clause or phrase in which no conjunction morpheme stands, no morpheme licenses that word and it is its own `added` unit under rule 30. Hebrew juxtaposes where English coordinates, and the ASV supplies the connective freely: `עַל־כָּתֵף תִּשָּׂא בָּעֲלָטָה תוֹצִיא` → *shalt thou bear it upon thy shoulder,* ***and*** *carry it forth in the dark* writes one for a clause the Hebrew leaves asyndetic, and `לְיוֹשְׁבֵי יְרוּשָׁלִַם אֶל־אַדְמַת יִשְׂרָאֵל` → *concerning the inhabitants of Jerusalem* ***and*** *the land of Israel* writes one for a second prepositional phrase the Hebrew merely sets beside the first. Do not fold such a word into the preposition, the verb or the noun standing next to it to avoid the `added`, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*: the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them, and a preposition whose own relation the ASV has left unstated is `unrepresented` under rule 40 rather than a home for a coordinator. Count the clause's conjunctions against the ASV's connectives, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, and mark whichever side is in surplus. **The apodosis connective is counted on exactly those terms, and the list of words that can carry it is as open as the connective list above.** Casuistic and temporal law writes its apodosis with a waw as often as without one, and the ASV writes a *then* either way, so read the Hebrew: `וְשָׁמְרוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶת־מִשְׁמֶרֶת יְהוָה` → ***then*** *the children of Israel kept the charge of Jehovah* gives *then* to the waw written for it, while `עַל־פִּי יְהוָה יַחֲנוּ` → ***then*** *according to the commandment of Jehovah they remained encamped* leaves the same word `added`, because that apodosis is juxtaposed with no conjunction in it at all. Do not give such a *then* to the preposition, the verb or the temporal phrase it stands beside, and do not read a waw the ASV has left unrendered as its home either: where the apodosis writes a waw and the ASV opens the clause bare, that waw is `unrepresented` under this rule's earlier sentence. Read the clause before counting, since a morpheme that has an English word of its own is not made a surplus by this sentence: a present negative carries a *nor* or a *neither* under rule 35, a `כִּי` or an `אִם` carries a *but* or an *or* the ASV has written for it, and only a connective no morpheme answers to is `added`. **And a coordinator standing inside one morpheme's own English rendering is not a connective supplied for the clause at all.** Where the ASV renders a single source morpheme by a fixed English phrase that contains an *and* or an *or*, the word coordinates the parts of that phrase and not two source items, so it belongs to that morpheme's unit, is neither `added` nor a separate connective, and does not move the unit's head, which rule 44 leaves on the lexical verb because a phrasal particle names nothing on its own. Decide it by asking what stands on either side of the English word in the Hebrew, which is the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use and the one rule 30 applies to its one-English-word condition. Where a source clause or phrase stands on each side, the preceding sentences govern and a connective no waw answers to is `added`; where the same one morpheme's rendering runs on both sides and no source item is coordinated at all, the word is written inside that rendering rather than beside it. `וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתוֹךְ אֲרָיוֹת` → *And he went up and down among the lions* keeps *up and down* whole with the one verb it renders, while `אָבְדָה תִקְוָתָהּ` → ***and*** *her hope was lost* leaves its supplied *and* `added`, because there a written clause stands on either side of it.
amendments.why: Rule 14's added-connective sentence enumerates 'a coordinating and, or or but', and its counting instruction two sentences later speaks generally of 'the ASV's connectives'. NUM.9 supplies the minimal pair that shows which reading is meant: 9.19 writes an apodosis waw and the ASV's then goes to it, while 9.20 writes the same clause with no conjunction at all and its then answers to nothing, with 9.21 and 9.13 showing the third case, a written waw the ASV leaves unrendered. A reader taking the enumeration as exhaustive would have folded 9.20's then into the preposition or the verb beside it, which the same sentence forbids for and. The widening adds no new principle and contradicts no corpus row: the corpus aligns a waw to then in 606 units, and added units carry no lemma, so nothing there speaks against it. Only the quoted sentence and the new worked pair are changed; every other clause of rule 14 is reproduced verbatim.

conventions: mo'ed rendered 'appointed season' is one substantive's multi-word rendering headed on 'appointed' under rule 31's subtraction, with 'season' named in each note as the available alternative. Applied at NUM.9.2, 9.3, 9.7 and 9.13; the suffix, where present, takes the possessive separately under rule 18.

The idiom beyn ha-'arbayim, rendered 'at even', is not rule 26's beyn X u-beyn Y: there is one beyn and no second member. The preposition takes the written 'at', the article is unrepresented because the ASV writes no 'the', and the dual noun takes 'even'. Applied at NUM.9.3, 9.5 and 9.11, and matched by the singular ba-'erev of NUM.9.15.

peh in the command formula is split or fused by what the ASV writes, not by the phrase. 'al-pi YHWH is three units, the preposition taking whatever word stands for it ('At', 'at', or the compound 'according to' as one rendering under rule 30), the construct noun taking 'the commandment' with a supplied 'the' under rule 29, and the name taking 'of Jehovah'. le-fi at NUM.9.17 instead meets rule 30's one-rendering condition and fuses with its preposition into 'whenever'. Likewise be-yad at NUM.9.23 fuses to 'by'.

The chapter's multi-morpheme temporal idioms are read as single fused renderings under rule 30 rather than split with parts unrepresented: yesh 'asher to 'sometimes' at NUM.9.20 and 9.21, headed on the existential particle; kol yeme 'asher to 'as long as' at NUM.9.18, headed on 'long', with the three-way split named in the note as the competing reading; and 'ish 'ish to 'any man' at NUM.9.10, headed on the noun, with the rule 22 split (first 'ish takes 'man' with its determiner, second unrepresented) named there.

Where the ASV reorders coordinated members, each connective morpheme is matched to the pair of members the English connective actually stands between, not taken in linear order. NUM.9.10 fronts lakhem 'o le-doroteikhem ahead of the journey clause, so the first written 'or' belongs to the second Hebrew 'o and the second 'or' to the first; NUM.9.1 does the same with the two dated phrases, giving the written 'in' to the month's preposition and the recast 'of' to the year's.

Where a source clause or phrase stands on each side, the preceding sentences govern and a connective no waw answers to is `added`; where the same one morpheme's rendering runs on both sides and no source item is coordinated at all, the word is written inside that rendering rather than beside it. `וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ בְּתוֹךְ אֲרָיוֹת` → *And he went up and down among the lions* keeps *up and down* whole with the one verb it renders, while `אָבְדָה תִקְוָתָהּ` → ***and*** *her hope was lost* leaves its supplied *and* `added`, because there a written clause stands on either side of it.
amended.why: Rule 14's added-connective sentence enumerates 'a coordinating and, or or but', and its counting instruction two sentences later speaks generally of 'the ASV's connectives'. NUM.9 supplies the minimal pair that shows which reading is meant: 9.19 writes an apodosis waw and the ASV's then goes to it, while 9.20 writes the same clause with no conjunction at all and its then answers to nothing, with 9.21 and 9.13 showing the third case, a written waw the ASV leaves unrendered. A reader taking the enumeration as exhaustive would have folded 9.20's then into the preposition or the verb beside it, which the same sentence forbids for and. The widening adds no new principle and contradicts no corpus row: the corpus aligns a waw to then in 606 units, and added units carry no lemma, so nothing there speaks against it. Only the quoted sentence and the new worked pair are changed; every other clause of rule 14 is reproduced verbatim.

report: Checked all 40 candidate lemma groups, and read the dump end to end for the splits the table cannot see, since it is keyed by source lemma and so blind to added units. Nothing is analysed two ways with the source licensing no difference, so patches is empty.

Apodosis connective: the one place the chapter looks inconsistent and is not. NUM.9.19 writes a waw before the apodosis and the ASV writes then, so the waw takes it; NUM.9.20 writes no conjunction at all before al-pi YHWH yachanu and its then is added; NUM.9.21 writes the waw but the ASV writes no connective there, so it is unrepresented. Three treatments resting on three different source-plus-English facts. NUM.9.13's unrendered apodosis waw is the same count.

Correlatives are handled alike in both places that have one: NUM.9.14 writes a waw before each of the two coordinated members and gives both to the first and and to the second; NUM.9.22 writes three 'o before three members and gives Whether, or, or one apiece. Both follow rule 14's 'o ... 'o sentence rather than hanging the pair on one morpheme, and NUM.9.14's note names the competing reading.

Other multi-treatment groups verified as ASV-licensed rather than split: be/le before an infinitive construct (9.19 when, 9.22 that, 9.4 that, 9.13 to, unrepresented in 9.6 and 9.22 where no function word is written); ba rendered in on the month phrase and of on the year phrase in 9.1, each matched to the English phrase it stands before; chuqqat ha-pesach counted identically in 9.12 and 9.14 under rule 29's arthrous case; the ha-...-ha-hu phrases in 9.3, 9.6, 9.7 and 9.13 all leaving both articles unrepresented because the written pronoun takes the one determiner; and nefesh to dead body headed on body beside matztzot to unleavened bread headed on unleavened, which is one subtraction test differing only in which English word carries the Hebrew lexeme.

BSB: no genuine error among the 25 disagreements. The Td x 15 and R x 4 runs are the documented convention difference (BSB attaches agreement articles and the le'mor lamed to their host words); the two 'ot markers in 9.3 and 9.11 are rule 16; the resumptive hu' of 9.13 is rule 22, two morphemes pointing at the antecedent with one English word written; and the three waws of 9.13 and 9.21 are apodosis waws the ASV leaves unrendered, which rule 14 requires be marked unrepresented. Nothing was changed to move the rate.

Five conventions recorded, all lexical or idiom judgments this chapter had to make and would otherwise be rediscovered. One amendment to rule 14: its added-connective sentence enumerates and, or and but, and this chapter supplies the minimal pair for a supplied then.
